To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ethanol production from corn requires 131% more fossil energy input than the energy content of ethanol produced, and that biodiesel production from soybeans requires 27% more fossil energy than the energy content in the biodiesel produced.

the energy cost to produce ethanol using corn is 1.3 units of fossil fuel energy for every unit of ethanol produced; the energy cost to make biodiesel fuel from soybeans is 2.7 units of fossil fuel for every unit of biodiesel produced; and the energy cost to generate biodiesel from sunflowers is 3.2 units of fossil fuel per unit of biodiesel.
the production of ethanol from corn requires 29% more fossil energy than the energy content of ethanol, while the production of ethanol using either switchgrass or wood results in a net energy gain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the entire production process of ethanol from corn and biodiesel from soybeans.
the production of biofuels using the most efficient and environmentally sound processes available.
the entire production process of ethanol from corn, switchgrass and wood; and biodiesel from soybeans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the production of ethanol and biodiesel fuels are not economically feasible, nor are they environmentally friendly.
the production of ethanol from corn and switchgrass and biodiesel from soybeans and sunflower are not energy efficient.
the production of ethanol from corn, switchgrass and wood is energy negative, i.e. more energy is used in the entire production process than is produced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ethanol production from corn, switchgrass and wood is energy negative.
ethanol and biodiesel production from biomass are energy intensive processes, and the energy inputs for ethanol and biodiesel are much larger than the energy outputs.
the production of ethanol from corn, switchgrass or wood, and biodiesel from soybeans or sunflower, are all energy intensive processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethanol and biodiesel production from renewable feedstock are not energy efficient and do not reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
the production of biodiesel and ethanol from renewable sources is not a viable solution to the energy problem.
the energy balance is negative for ethanol production from corn, and that it is positive for ethanol production from switchgrass and wood.
